sentences.text: The skull of this creature was 235 millimeters long, low, elongated, and finished with a rounded tip.
It possessed at least 27 teeth on each side of both jaws, with large front pairs forming a sharp mesh.
Scientists estimated its wingspan to be around 1.45 meters.
The front nine pairs of teeth were especially large and created a sharp interlocking pattern.
Its name combines Greek words meaning 'northern' and 'wing'.
Paleontologists Lü Junchang and Ji Qiang named the genus in 2005.
The type species is Boreopterus cuiae, a name chosen to honor a person named Cui Xu.
David Unwin interpreted this animal as a soaring creature similar to modern albatrosses and frigatebirds.
It has been suggested that it foraged by swimming and trapping small prey with its needle-like teeth, similar to modern Platanista dolphins.
When first described in 2006, it was placed in the family Ornithocheiridae, a view supported by David Unwin.
In 2006, Lü published an analysis placing it as the sister taxon of Feilongus within the new family Boreopteridae.
A 2018 study by Nicholas Longrich and colleagues restricted the family Boreopteridae to only Boreopterus and Zhenyuanopterus.
Fossils come from the Lower Cretaceous Yixian Formation in Dalian, Liaoning, China.
It lived between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago during the Barremian to Aptian stages.
Some researchers have suggested that the related genus Zhenyuanopterus represents the adult stage of Boreopterus.
